questions.question: Explain how the tilt of the Earth's axis causes day length to change through the year, and why places on the equator have about twelve hours of daylight all year.
questions.expected_answer: Because the axis is tilted, the circle of illumination does not usually pass through the poles, so it cuts each parallel unequally. In December the Southern Hemisphere leans towards the sun, so more than half of each southern parallel is lit and days are longer than 12 hours; in June it leans away and days are shorter. At the equinoxes every parallel is cut in half and day and night are equal. The equator is a great circle, always cut exactly in half by the circle of illumination, so it has about 12 hours of daylight all year.

questions.question: Use the day-length figures for Musina, Cape Town and London to state the rule linking latitude and the seasonal change in day length. What happens at the poles?
questions.expected_answer: Musina, at about 22°S, swings by under three hours; Cape Town, at about 34°S, by about four and a half hours; London, at about 51,5°N, by nearly nine hours. The further a place is from the equator, the greater the difference between its summer and winter day lengths. At the poles there are about six months of continuous daylight and about six months of continuous darkness.

questions.question: Explain the two effects that make summer warmer than winter, and explain the seasonal lag with an example.
questions.expected_answer: In summer the midday sun is higher, so its rays concentrate energy on a smaller area and pass through less atmosphere; and the days are longer, so the ground is heated for more hours and cools for fewer. In winter both effects reverse. The seasonal lag: land and sea store heat, so after the December solstice the hemisphere keeps gaining more heat than it loses for several weeks, and January and February are usually hotter than December; similarly July is colder than June.
